title: Modi Invites Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman to BRICS Summit in New Delhi
excerpt: India extends formal invitation to Bangladesh's prime minister for the 18th BRICS Summit in September, signalling a diplomatic thaw after months of strained ties between the South Asian neighbours.
body:
• Indian PM Narendra Modi has invited Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman to the 18th BRICS Summit, scheduled for 12-13 September in New Delhi.
  • Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed the invitation has been forwarded to the Prime Minister's Office, though no decision on attendance has been announced.
  • The invitation comes amid a broader diplomatic recalibration between Delhi and Dhaka following Tarique Rahman's election as prime minister in February 2026.
  • India is hosting the BRICS Summit under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" and plans to invite several non-member nations as special guests.

India Extends BRICS Invite to Dhaka

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has formally invited Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to attend the 18th BRICS Summit, scheduled for 12-13 September in New Delhi, Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed on Wednesday.

https://x.com/RT_India_news/status/2080292896901902712

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told reporters that the ministry had received the invitation from India and forwarded it to the Prime Minister's Office. No decision has yet been announced on whether Rahman will attend, according to The Business Standard.

Bangladesh is not a member of the 11-nation BRICS bloc, but as the summit host, India is expected to invite several non-member countries as special guests. The summit's theme — "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" — reflects what New Delhi describes as a people-centric and humanity-first approach to multilateral cooperation.

A Relationship Under Repair

The invitation carries weight beyond diplomatic protocol. India-Bangladesh relations have been on a slow path to normalisation after a turbulent period that began with the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government in August 2024 and the subsequent violence against minorities, particularly the Hindu community.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DaAh50-OGCB/

The outgoing interim government under Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was perceived in India as less aligned with New Delhi's strategic interests. Delhi largely avoided engaging with the Yunus administration, viewing it as an unelected government, according to analysts cited by LiveMint.

The dynamic shifted after the Bangladesh Nationalist Party's (BNP) decisive victory in parliamentary elections earlier this year. Modi extended "warmest congratulations" to Rahman upon his swearing-in as prime minister on 17 February, sending a personal letter through Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla inviting Rahman and his family to visit India.

"As two close neighbours, India and Bangladesh have a deep-rooted friendship founded on shared history, cultural ties and the aspirations of our peoples for peace and prosperity."

— Narendra Modi, Indian Prime Minister, in his letter to Tarique Rahman

Diplomatic Signals From Dhaka

Bangladesh's response to the BRICS invitation was measured but pointed. When asked about bilateral ties, State Minister Shama Obaed Islam stressed that Bangladesh, as a democratic country with a democratically elected government, wants peace and stability across the region.

"This is our position, and we want peace and stability to be maintained in our region," she said, adding that Dhaka hopes India, "as a major democratic country, would address the concerns of its people through democratic means" — a veiled reference to India's domestic political tensions that Bangladesh has been watching closely.

The minister also flagged the upcoming visit of US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor, which she said is expected to open a new chapter in Bangladesh-US relations — underscoring Dhaka's interest in broadening its diplomatic relationships beyond any single partner.

What the BRICS Platform Means for Bangladesh

For the Bangladeshi diaspora and Indian community alike, the BRICS invitation carries practical implications. A face-to-face meeting between Modi and Rahman on the summit's sidelines could unlock progress on long-stalled bilateral issues: water-sharing agreements, trade imbalances, border management, and the status of minority communities — concerns that directly affect families with ties on both sides of the border.

India's BRICS presidency has been ambitious. The foreign ministers of BRICS member states met in Delhi in mid-May, and the September summit will bring together leaders from member nations including Brazil, China, Russia, South Africa, and newer members like Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the UAE. For India, inviting Bangladesh fits a strategy of positioning New Delhi as a regional anchor with reach beyond the bloc's formal membership.

Rahman's own agenda has been equally outward-looking. On the same day the BRICS invitation was confirmed, he addressed the FICCI FDI Conference 2026 in Dhaka, pledging to build a $1 trillion economy by 2034 through investment-friendly reforms and calling on global investors to become "long-term partners in Bangladesh's economic transformation."

What to Watch

The key question now is whether Rahman will accept the invitation. His attendance at the September summit would mark his first major multilateral engagement hosted by India and could set the tone for a reset in Delhi-Dhaka relations. Reports earlier this year had suggested a potential bilateral visit was in the works, with Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman expected to lead a delegation to India focused on border stability, counter-terrorism cooperation, and maritime security.

For now, the invitation itself is the signal — India is reaching out, and Dhaka is at least keeping the door open.
nri_angle: A Modi-Rahman meeting at the BRICS Summit could advance progress on border management, minority community protections, and bilateral trade — issues that directly affect the Indian and Bangladeshi diaspora communities with family ties on both sides.
